clue.text: After memory's stirred up, one cultivated fictional villain

indicators.note: in a down clue, stirred up means the letters are lifted and read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: ROM is read-only memory in a computer
the Roman numeral for one is I
arty means having pretensions to culture

explanation.surface: A villain is grown or bred once someone's memory is jogged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stirred up' turns ROM (computer memory) upwards into MOR in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Professor Moriarty is Sherlock Holmes's arch-enemy in Conan Doyle's stories, a villain of fiction.

clue.text: Back problem the source of red swelling

indicators.note: back tells us the word for problem is read in reverse

parts.note: 'there's the rub' - a rub is a difficulty or problem

indicators.note: the source of a word is where it starts, so take its opening letter

explanation.surface: A doctor names a back complaint that started off a red swelling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' turns RUB into BUR; 'the source of' red gives R.
explanation.definitionFit: A burr is a rough knot or lump, a swelling growing on a tree trunk.

clue.text: Is it like a dramatist to work repeatedly in basement? Not half

indicators.note: to work these letters is to knead them into a new shape
repeatedly tells us the little word in is taken twice
not half of the word basement leaves its first half only

explanation.surface: A question whether a playwright's habit is to keep working down in a basement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half' of BASEMENT gives BASE; with ININ ('in' 'repeatedly') those letters are rearranged ('to work').
explanation.definitionFit: Henrik Ibsen was the Norwegian dramatist, and the adjective describes things in his style.

clue.text: Discussed navigating competition for explorer

indicators.note: discussed means spoken out, so we want a word that sounds like the phrase

parts.note: a rally is a motoring competition in which drivers and navigators follow a route

explanation.surface: People talk over a navigation contest for explorers.
explanation.walkthrough: The explorer's surname is commonly said like 'rally'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Walter Raleigh was an Elizabethan adventurer who sailed to the Americas.

clue.text: Knocked back the Italian lolly, as it melted?

indicators.note: knocked back, as a drink is swallowed, here means the article is turned around

parts.note: il is the Italian word for the
lolly is British slang for money, and a quid is a pound

explanation.surface: Someone gulps down an Italian ice lolly as it starts to melt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocked back' reverses IL to LI. An ice lolly that melts turns runny.
explanation.definitionFit: A melted lolly is no longer solid but flowing, so the definition describes that state by example.

clue.text: Army leader's gone with Tommy, moving around river

indicators.note: around means the rearranged letters are placed around the river's letter
moving means the letters are shifted about into a fresh order

parts.note: R is the standard abbreviation for river on maps

explanation.surface: An army commander has left, taking a British soldier who wanders by a river.
explanation.walkthrough: Tommy is slang for a British soldier, so the surface reads as troops on the move; the soldier is only letters here.
explanation.definitionFit: Field Marshal Montgomery commanded the British Eighth Army at El Alamein.

clue.text: Record company clipped part of newspaper article on AC/DC

indicators.note: in an across clue, on means placed after, so the article comes last
clipped means the word is cut short by its last letter

parts.note: a column is a section of a newspaper
AC/DC is slang for bisexual, shortened to bi
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A record label trimmed a piece of press coverage about the rock band AC/DC.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clipped' cuts N from COLUMN. AC/DC looks like the band but is slang for bisexual.
explanation.definitionFit: Columbia is a long-established American record label, so it is an example of a record company.

clue.text: Tipster regularly circulating dated legendary princess

indicators.note: circulating means going around, so these letters wrap the other word
regularly means take every other letter of the word

parts.note: dated means old

explanation.surface: A racing tipster passes round outdated tips about a princess from legend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes I, S, E from Tipster, and 'circulating' puts them round OLD.
explanation.definitionFit: Isolde is the Irish princess of the Tristan legend, loved by the knight Tristan.

clue.text: Port finally passed across

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of passed

parts.note: over means across, as in going over a bridge

explanation.surface: Someone at last crossed over to a harbour town.
explanation.definitionFit: Dover is the English Channel port in Kent, the main ferry crossing to France.

clue.text: Frenchman's tart securing boob

indicators.note: securing means holding something firmly inside

parts.note: a tart is a kind of pie
a boob is a mistake, and to err is to make one

explanation.surface: A French pastry chef's tart holds a blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: Boob here is British slang for a blunder, not anatomy.
explanation.definitionFit: Pierre is a typical French first name, so it stands for a man from France.

clue.text: Low grade rugby training? This writer's describing St Helens maybe

parts.note: E is a low exam grade
RU is Rugby Union
PT is physical training
this writer has, from the setter's view, is I have, written I've

explanation.surface: The setter reports poor-quality rugby practice in the town of St Helens.
explanation.walkthrough: St Helens is a rugby league town in England, but here Mount St Helens, the volcano in Washington State, is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: Mount St Helens is a volcano that blew in 1980, so it is described by this adjective for bursting out.

clue.text: Crew attacked by man on board causing devastation

indicators.note: attacked means battered about, so its letters get reshuffled

parts.note: the king is a chess piece, a man on the chessboard

explanation.surface: A ship's crew is assaulted by someone aboard, wreaking havoc.
explanation.walkthrough: 'attacked' rearranges CREW. 'man on board' looks like a sailor but is a chess piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Wreaking havoc is ruinous destruction, a direct synonym of laying waste.

clue.text: Dance daily on street during Christmas when retired

parts.note: a daily is a British cleaner who comes in each day, also called a char

indicators.note: during means placed within the other word
retired means going back, so the word reads in reverse

parts.note: Noel is Christmas

explanation.surface: A cleaner dances in the street over Christmas after retiring.
explanation.walkthrough: A daily is a British cleaner who comes in by the day; 'when retired' reverses the Christmas word to LEON.
explanation.definitionFit: The Charleston is a lively 1920s jazz-age dance.

clue.text: Entrance contains parcels at the back — a delivery to nightwatchman?

indicators.note: contains means holds another letter inside

parts.note: a door is an entrance

indicators.note: at the back points to the final letter of parcels

explanation.surface: A doorway full of parcels as a night guard takes a delivery.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a nightwatchman is a lower-order batter sent in late in the day; 'delivery' is a bowled ball, not a parcel.
explanation.definitionFit: A doosra is an off-spinner's ball that turns the other way, the kind of delivery any batter might face.

clue.text: Country's right-wing blocking radio once — in such a regime?

indicators.note: blocking means standing in the way, inside the other word

parts.note: tranny was a dated term for a transistor radio

indicators.note: the right wing of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: A nation's right wing jams old radio broadcasts, typical of an oppressive state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'right-wing' gives Y, the end of Country; 'blocking' sits it inside TRANNY.
explanation.definitionFit: Jamming broadcasts is what a despotic government does, so the regime is a despotism.

clue.text: Bird rejuvenated by new iPhone attached

indicators.note: attached means the times sign is tacked on to the end
new means the letters are made over in a fresh order

parts.note: by is the times sign, x, as in three by four

explanation.surface: A bird is revived by being connected to a new smartphone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' rearranges IPHONE; 'by' is X as in measurements, 'attached' at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: The mythical phoenix is reborn from its own ashes, a bird renewed again and again.

clue.text: Welcome monarch and roguish chief priest

parts.note: hi is a greeting
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the Queen
arch means mischievous or roguish

explanation.surface: A priest greets the monarch and a mischievous senior cleric.
explanation.definitionFit: A hierarch is a high priest or senior church leader, someone at the top of a religious order.

clue.text: Accepted free gins procured by Poles — they often hang around pubs

parts.note: in means accepted or fashionable

indicators.note: free means released from order, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: N and S are the north and south poles

explanation.surface: Free drinks bought by Polish people, who tend to loiter round pubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'free' rearranges GINS to NSIG. 'Poles' looks like nationality but means compass points.
explanation.definitionFit: Pub signboards hang from the front of British pubs, so they literally hang about them.

clue.text: Agreement opposing fellow vacating number 28

parts.note: con means against, as in pros and cons
co- is the prefix for a fellow, as in co-worker

indicators.note: vacating means emptying out, leaving only the outer letters

parts.note: the clue numbered 28 across in this puzzle, the London district

explanation.surface: An agreement against a man moving out of house number 28.
explanation.walkthrough: 'number 28' points to the answer at 28 across; 'vacating' empties it, leaving its first and last letters R and D.
explanation.definitionFit: Concord means harmony or a treaty between parties, a synonym for agreement.

clue.text: Worn-out US agent, upset inside

indicators.note: inside means one word is placed within the other

parts.note: a fed is an FBI agent in US slang
to ail is to trouble or upset

explanation.surface: An exhausted American agent is troubled within.
explanation.definitionFit: Failed can mean weakened or broken down, as of health or machinery that has given out.

clue.text: Blue street map you're picking up

indicators.note: picking up means hearing a sound, so the words are heard as they are said

parts.note: the A-Z is a London street atlas, followed by you're

explanation.surface: Someone, gloomy, is collecting a road map.
explanation.walkthrough: The A-Z is the standard British street atlas; 'A-Z you're' said quickly sounds like the colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Azure is a bright sky blue, a shade of the colour.

clue.text: Sudden verse reveals US male singer

indicators.note: reveals means the words display a name concealed within them

explanation.surface: An unexpected verse unmasks an American singer.
explanation.definitionFit: John Denver was an American country-folk singer, known for Take Me Home, Country Roads.

clue.text: How many spectators enter ground? Eleven perhaps

definitions.meaning: how fans pass through a turnstile: singly, in sequence
the numeral 11 looks like a 1 beside a 1

explanation.definitionFit: Crowds pass turnstiles singly, and the figures of eleven are a pair of ones side by side.

clue.text: With lad in charge, coach returned at such speed? Definitely

indicators.note: returned means going back, so the vehicle's word reads in reverse

parts.note: a coach is a bus
a son is a lad

explanation.surface: A coach and his boy head home; it was slow, slower than sound certainly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' reverses BUS. The definition is cheeky: a coach certainly travels slower than sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Below the speed of sound describes every bus, so the definition is a playful affirmation.

clue.text: Old car manufacturer's Sierra built with varying metal front and rear

parts.note: the metal at the front is gold, chemical symbol Au
Sierra is S in the NATO phonetic alphabet
the metal at the rear is tin

explanation.surface: A defunct carmaker builds a Ford Sierra with different metal bumpers front and back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'varying metal' means the metal differs: gold (AU) at the front, tin at the rear. The Sierra was a Ford car.
explanation.definitionFit: Austin was a British motor company that made the Mini and Seven, now gone.

clue.text: All pee in local bog

parts.note: sum means the whole, all of it
pee is how the letter P is spelt out

explanation.surface: Everyone relieves themselves in a nearby toilet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bog' looks like British slang for a toilet, but means marshy ground.
explanation.definitionFit: In dialect a sump is a boggy pool or marsh; local marks it as regional usage.

clue.text: Author, first person in L'Equipe to pen extra retrospective

indicators.note: to pen is to shut in, so the French pronoun encloses the other letters

parts.note: je is the French for I, and L'Equipe is a French newspaper

indicators.note: retrospective means looking backwards, so the word is reversed

parts.note: more means extra

explanation.surface: A writer, the first person on a French sports paper, writes up a bonus review.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retrospective' reverses MORE to EROM, which JE pens.
explanation.definitionFit: Jerome K Jerome wrote the comic novel Three Men in a Boat.

clue.text: Loaded Lambretta rider, say, bypasses northern part of London

parts.note: loaded is slang for rich

indicators.note: bypasses means goes round, so these letters surround the other

parts.note: mods were a 1960s British youth subculture who rode Lambretta scooters

explanation.surface: A wealthy scooter rider skirts the northern part of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Richmond is a riverside borough in south-west London.
